catalog_quote: From this example it can be seen that in Batak stress is distinctive and hence is a phoneme. In Batak the stress generally falls on the penult. When an utterance with penultimate stress is expanded by means of affixes, the stress, if necessary, moves to the new penult. ... Exceptions to this general rule can be found in words derived from monosyllables when the base is the last syllable, and in loanwords of recent borrowing. In these words the stress falls on the ultima ... When otherwise the stress does not fall on the penult, it is to signal a change in content or as in some cases as a result of an ellipsis. One function of the shift of stress is, as above, to contrast a noun with the corresponding 'group VII' modifier. Other examples of this are: /gájjaŋ/ - 'length', and /gajjáŋ/ - 'long' ... sweep_summary: One item only (Roosman 2006, LOT 129), already held by the project and already in the per-language bibliography; re-read at sec. 2.3.2 and ch. III. It is about word stress of this language and CONFIRMS the catalog's set by morphology coding from Nababan 1981: penult for nouns/verbs, stress shifting to the new penult under suffixation, final stress for predicative adjectives and comparative -an, attributive/na-adjectives penult; her own acoustic experiment on eight penult-stressed TB words finds the rise-fall pitch accent anchored on the penultimate syllable and stress cued by pitch, not duration. Her description is explicitly 'mainly based on Nababan (1981)', so it does not supersede the catalog source. Nothing left to acquire from the item list. no open copy located): Chen, P. (1984) 'Stress in Toba Batak' and Emmorey (1984) on TB intonation, both in Schachter (ed.), Studies in the Structure of Toba Batak, UCLA Occasional Papers in Linguistics 5 - Chen would be the best first-hand acoustic statement (medium priority; the catalog classification does not depend on it).

new_statements.quote: Stress in TB is penultimate for nouns and verbs containing two or more syllables and final for predicatively used adjectives (Nababan, 1981; Emmorey, 1984). There is a clear difference, for instance, between N tíbo ‘height’ and A tibó ‘high’ (stressed syllable indicated by acute accent mark). However, attributive adjectives, and adjectives following na (relative pronoun), do not have final stress; they have penultimate stress, e.g. na tíbo ‘which is high’. ... If words with penultimate stress are suffixed, stress shifts to the next syllable in order to keep the stress penultimate.

new_statements.reading: Default penultimate stress on nouns and verbs that stays on the penult under suffixation, with final stress assigned by grammatical class (predicative adjectives, comparative -an) - i.e. stress position depends on word class and morphology, not on syllable count or weight alone, exactly the catalog's set by morphology coding. Roosman's summary is avowedly derived from Nababan (1981), the catalog's deciding source, and adds only an instrumental confirmation that the eight penult-stressed nouns/verbs she measured carry the F0 rise-fall on the penultimate syllable and that stress is cued by pitch rather than lengthening.

sources.note: Second-hand summary (explicitly 'mainly based on Nababan (1981)'): TB has distinctive lexical stress; penultimate for nouns and verbs of 2+ syllables, final for predicative adjectives (tíbo 'height' vs tibó 'high'; ítom 'your brother/sister' vs itóm 'black'), attributive and na-adjectives penultimate; suffixation moves stress to the new penult (dálan, mardálan, daláni, dalánna); compounds and phrases carry one main stress on the final constituent (hòda pácu); comparative -an takes final stress (úli vs ulián); Nababan's loudness claim and secondary stress in borumuna noted.
